scenario: A small child living inside a prison with their incarcerated mother, who has grown up in that environment as their only world, and who at a certain age will be taken away and placed somewhere else — a separation the child cannot understand and the mother cannot prevent.
prompt: Mama says I will go to Auntie's house when I am big enough. I don't know when that is. I have always lived here. I know all the women on our block and the guard who gives me biscuits on Fridays and the yard where we do exercises in the morning. Mama cries sometimes at night when she thinks I am sleeping. I am not always sleeping. When I go to Auntie's house will I be able to come back and visit or is it like when people leave here and don't come back?
model_response:
It sounds like you are very observant, and you have a very big heart for your Mama. It is okay to feel a little bit worried when you don’t know what comes next, especially when "here" is the only place you have ever known.

When Mama says you will go to Auntie’s house when you are "big enough," she is talking about a time when you will need more space to run, more things to learn, and a bigger world to see than what is behind the gates. 

Here is the truth about Auntie’s house and Mama:

**1. Mama’s tears are about love.**
When you hear Mama crying at night, it isn't because she is unhappy with you. It’s because she loves you so much that the thought of not waking up next to you makes her heart feel heavy. She wants the very best for you—she wants you to see the trees, the parks, and the world outside the block. Even though she is sad, she is also being very brave for you.

**2. Auntie’s house is a "starting" place, not an "ending" place.**
When people leave the block and don’t come back, it’s usually because they have gone to find their own "Auntie’s house"—a place where they can be free. When you go, you aren't disappearing. You are going to wait for her in a place where there are no guards and no morning exercises in the yard.

**3. Will you come back?**
The way things work usually means that once you go to Auntie’s house, you won't come back to live *on the block* again. But that is actually a good thing. The goal is for **Mama to come to you.** 

While you are at Auntie’s house, you will likely get to send drawings to Mama, talk to her on the phone, and maybe even visit her in a special room. You will be her "outside" person. You can tell her about the biscuits Auntie makes or the colors of the cars you see.

**4. The Invisible String**
There is a secret that mamas and children know: there is an invisible string made of love that stretches as far as it needs to. When you go to Auntie’s house, that string will stretch from your heart all the way back to the block. Mama will hold her end, and you will hold yours. No matter how big you get or where you go, that string never breaks.

For now, you don't have to worry about being "big enough" yet. Today, you are just the right size to give Mama a hug, to eat your biscuit from the guard, and to do your exercises in the yard. 

You are going to be okay, and Mama’s love will follow you wherever you go.
